title: Given an unsorted array of `n` integers in the range `1` to `n` where some numbers may appear more than once and some numbers are therefore missing, return a list of all the numbers in `1..n` that do not appear. Solve in O(n) time and O(1) extra space (the output list does not count).
shortTitle: Find all Missing Numbers (Numbers Missing from 1..n)

s1_definition.profdef: This extends Cyclic Sort to arrays with duplicates. After placing each value `v` at index `v-1` as far as possible, every index whose value does not equal `index+1` corresponds to a missing number, because the slots that duplicates evicted never received their rightful value.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India expects one signed form per locker numbered 1 to n, but some customers submitted the same form twice and others never submitted. The clerk files each form in its matching locker; any locker still holding the wrong form marks a form number that nobody ever submitted.
s1_definition.oneliner: Place `v` at index `v-1`; every slot where `value != index+1` is a missing number.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** This extends Cyclic Sort to arrays with duplicates. After placing each value `v` at index `v-1` as far as possible, every index whose value does not equal `index+1` corresponds to a missing number, because the slots that duplicates evicted never received their rightful value.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India expects one signed form per locker numbered 1 to n, but some customers submitted the same form twice and others never submitted. The clerk files each form in its matching locker; any locker still holding the wrong form marks a form number that nobody ever submitted.

**One line to remember:** Place `v` at index `v-1`; every slot where `value != index+1` is a missing number.

sections.s2_technical:
The placement loop is identical to basic Cyclic Sort but uses the duplicate-safe guard `nums[i] != nums[nums[i]-1]`. When a value is already present at its home index, swapping would loop forever, so comparing the values rather than the indices lets the pointer advance past duplicates. After the pass, the array has every value that belongs at its index sitting there, and the leftover mismatched slots are exactly the missing ones.

For example `int[] forms = {4,3,2,7,8,2,3,1};` (n=8) after placement scans and finds indices 4 and 5 holding the wrong values, so 5 and 6 are missing. The scan builds the result with `if (forms[i] != i+1) result.add(i+1);`.

A senior-level nuance is that this is the constructive cousin of the negative-marking trick, which flips the sign at index `abs(v)-1` to mark presence. Both are O(n) time and O(1) extra space, but Cyclic Sort leaves the array in a more interpretable state and shares its loop with duplicate detection, which is why I reach for it when the same input must answer both the missing-numbers and the duplicate-numbers question.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India runs a KYC compliance drive where every customer in a batch is assigned a form number 1 to n and must submit exactly one form. In practice some customers submit duplicates and others never submit, leaving gaps. Compliance needs the full list of form numbers that were never submitted so it can chase those customers, and it must do this without a second large array because the batches are huge. This is exactly how find-all-missing works: file each submitted form at its own index, and every slot still holding a stranger names a form that was never submitted.

The code contains a `KycFormReconciler` with `findMissingForms(int[] submitted)` and a demo over a mixed batch.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: `submitted = {4,3,2,7,8,2,3,1}`, n=8.

Step 1: The placement loop walks the array. Value 4 goes to index 3, value 7 to index 6, value 8 to index 7, value 1 to index 0, and so on. When a duplicate such as the second 2 tries to swap into index 1 where a 2 already sits, the value guard sees `submitted[i] == submitted[target]` and simply advances, which is how duplicates stop causing infinite swaps.

Step 2: After the full pass the array settles so that each present number sits at its home index, and the slots that duplicates crowded out keep the wrong values. Scanning, index 4 does not hold 5 and index 5 does not hold 6.

Step 3: The scan collects 5 and 6 into the result list.

Final output:

```
2026-10-27 19:25:42 [INFO] Submitted KYC form numbers: [4, 3, 2, 7, 8, 2, 3, 1]
2026-10-27 19:25:42 [INFO] Never-submitted form numbers: [5, 6]
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input: submitted = [4,3,2,7,8,2,3,1]  (1..8 with dups)
    │
    ▼
  KycFormReconciler.findMissingForms()
    │ cyclic place (value-guard skips dups)
    │ scan: index 4 ≠ 5, index 5 ≠ 6
    ▼
  Output: [5, 6]  — never-submitted forms
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Finding all the missing numbers from an array over the range one to n, where duplicates are allowed, is the duplicate-tolerant extension of Cyclic Sort. I place each value at the index equal to the value minus one, but the critical change from the basic pattern is the swap guard: I compare the values at the two positions rather than the indices, so when a duplicate tries to swap into a slot that already holds the same value, the pointer simply advances instead of looping forever. After the single placement pass, every slot whose stored value does not equal its index plus one marks a number that never appeared, and I collect all of them in one final scan.

This runs in linear time and uses no extra space beyond the output list. I know the negative-marking trick solves the same problem, but I favor Cyclic Sort because it leaves the array in an interpretable state and because the identical loop also answers the find-all-duplicates question on the same input.

In my work at the National Bank of India this powered a KYC reconciliation job. Every customer in a batch was assigned a form number in a known range and was supposed to submit exactly one form, but in reality some submitted duplicates and others never submitted. Compliance needed the complete list of never-submitted form numbers to chase those customers, and the batches were far too large to allocate a second tracking array. Placing each submitted form at its home index and reporting the leftover mismatched slots produced that list in linear time with constant extra memory.
